screens.title: Method Overriding and the @Override Annotation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how subclasses change inherited behavior through method overriding and why that matters for polymorphism and clean code. Overriding lets a subclass provide a specific implementation for a method defined in its superclass while keeping the same method signature, which preserves polymorphic calls. For example, an Animal class can define a generic makeSound method while Dog and Cat subclasses override it to bark or meow. You will also learn the practical rules that govern overriding: matching signature, compatible return types including covariant returns, access modifier constraints, and rules about checked exceptions. Equally important is the @Override annotation — it tells the compiler you intend to override and prevents subtle errors that would otherwise create overloaded or new methods by accident. Throughout the screens you’ll see concrete code examples, a hands-on vehicle exercise, and common mistakes you can spot during code reviews. By the end, you’ll be able to override methods correctly, call super when appropriate, and use @Override to catch errors early. Think about one superclass method you would want to change in your own codebase — how would a subclass improve it?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to tell overriding and overloading apart and apply the right technique in your code. You will practice writing subclass methods that match a superclass signature and use covariant return types when appropriate. You will also use the @Override annotation as a compile-time check so small typos or signature mismatches surface immediately instead of silently changing behavior. Finally, you will learn the rules about access modifiers and checked exceptions in overriding and how to call the superclass implementation with super. method() to extend, not replace, inherited behavior. Each objective pairs a definition with a short why-it-matters example so you can see immediate value: for instance, overriding makeSound() in an Animal hierarchy makes polymorphic code expressive and predictable. These skills reduce runtime surprises and make code easier to maintain and review. Practice and the included hands-on exercises will reinforce how to recognize mistakes and protect your intent with @Override.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills and mental checks you should adopt. You will practice calling super. method() from a subclass to reuse and then augment behavior. For example, a Book subclass can call super. displayItemDetails() to print common fields and then add author and page-count lines. You will also learn to identify common mistakes: mismatched parameter lists cause overloading, wrong return types break overriding unless covariant returns are used, and making the overriding method less accessible will generate compile errors. These habits catch many class-hierarchy bugs early.

Hands-on habits
Annotate overrides, compile early, and prefer calling super when extending behavior. These habits reduce regressions and make your intent explicit for reviewers.
Habit: Add @Override above methods you expect to override.

Quick checklist

screens.title: What is Method Overriding?
screens.narratorSegment: Method overriding is the mechanism where a subclass provides a specific implementation for a method already declared in its superclass, keeping the same method signature. The purpose is to let different concrete types respond differently to the same polymorphic call. For a concrete picture, imagine an Animal class with a makeSound method that prints a generic message. A Dog subclass overrides makeSound to print a bark string, and a Cat subclass overrides it to print a meow. When code holds a reference of type Animal to a Dog instance and calls makeSound, the Dog version runs because Java uses dynamic dispatch at runtime. Overriding supports polymorphism: you can write generic code that treats many subclasses uniformly while each subclass implements its own behavior. A common misconception is thinking that simply defining a method with the same name in a subclass is enough; the signature must match exactly to be overriding, or else you’ve silently created a different method. This silent creation of a new method is dangerous because calls through superclass references will not use your intended implementation. Takeaway: overriding preserves the method contract while changing behavior — that contract is what lets polymorphism work reliably.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Overriding = subclass method with the same signature replacing or extending superclass behavior; enables polymorphism.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is Method Overriding?
Definition

Change inherited behavior while preserving the contract

Overriding preserves the method signature while allowing subclasses to implement behavior that matches their concrete semantics. This is essential for polymorphism and runtime dispatch.

Concrete example
// Superclass
class Animal {
  public void makeSound() {
    System.out.println("Animal makes a sound.");
  }
}

// Subclass overrides
class Dog extends Animal {
  @Override
  public void makeSound() {
    System.out.println("Dog barks: woof!");
  }
}

// Runtime dispatch
Animal a = new Dog();
a.makeSound(); // Dog barks: woof!
Common misconceptions
  • Same method name alone does not guarantee overriding — parameters and return type must match the signature.
  • Using a narrower access modifier in the subclass creates a compile error, not an override.
  • Forgetting @Override may silently allow overloading instead of overriding.
Key Takeaway

Overriding lets subclasses replace behavior without changing how callers invoke the method; matching the signature is essential.

screens.title: Signature Rules for Overriding
screens.narratorSegment: For a method in a subclass to override a superclass method, the signature must match: same method name and the same number, types, and order of parameters. The return type must be compatible. Java allows covariant return types: the overriding method may return a subtype of the original return type. For example, if a superclass method returns java. lang. Number, a subclass override can return java. lang. Integer. This preserves substitutability because every Integer is a Number, but not every Number is an Integer. Another rule is that generic type erasure can affect signatures — but your practical check is simple: the compiler will accept a covariant return only when it is type-safe. A useful mental model is: overriding keeps the contract consumers expect, while a covariant return type narrows what the caller actually gets at runtime in a safe way. A common mistake is changing parameter types or order; that creates an overloaded method, not an overridden one, and calls through superclass references will still invoke the original method. Always compile and run a small test that calls the method via a superclass reference to confirm the override.

keyIdea.title: Signature checklist
keyIdea.text: Match name and parameters exactly; return type must be compatible — covariant returns are allowed when safe.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Signature Rules
Rules
  1. Same name and parameter list in the same order and types.
  2. Return type must be compatible; covariant returns (subtypes) are allowed.
  3. Access modifier cannot be more restrictive than the superclass method.
  4. Cannot throw broader checked exceptions than the overridden method.
Practical check: write a small runtime test that invokes the method via a superclass reference to confirm the subclass implementation actually runs.
Covariant return example
// Superclass
class Factory {
  public Number create() { return 0; }
}

// Subclass returns a subtype
class IntegerFactory extends Factory {
  @Override
  public Integer create() { return 1; }
}
Misconception check: returning a completely unrelated type or widening the return is not allowed and will not compile. Covariant returns must preserve the is-a relationship.

screens.title: Access Modifiers and Exception Rules
screens.narratorSegment: Two important constraints often catch learners by surprise: access modifiers and checked exceptions. When a subclass overrides a method, it cannot use a more restrictive access modifier than the superclass method. For instance, if the superclass method is protected, the subclass method can be protected or public, but not private. This rule maintains substitutability for callers with different visibility. For exceptions, an overriding method cannot declare checked exceptions that are broader than those declared by the overridden method. If the superclass method declares to throw IOException, the overriding method may declare to throw FileNotFoundException, which is narrower, or declare no checked exceptions. Declaring a broader checked exception would break callers that rely on the original contract. A helpful contrast: unchecked exceptions (runtime exceptions) are not checked by this rule, so they can be thrown freely, but you should still be careful to preserve A P I expectations. A common mistake is making an overriding method private or adding a broad checked exception; both generate compile-time errors. The safe habit is to mirror or relax visibility and restrict checked exceptions to compatible or narrower types.

keyIdea.title: Visibility & Exceptions
keyIdea.text: Do not make an overriding method less visible; do not widen checked exceptions — both break substitutability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Access & Exceptions
Access modifier rules
Allowed
  • public -> public
  • protected -> protected or public
Disallowed
  • public -> protected or private
  • protected -> private
Misconception: making the override private doesn’t hide the superclass method — it causes a compile error because callers expecting the superclass contract would lose access.
Checked exceptions rule

The overriding method cannot declare checked exceptions that are broader than those declared in the overridden method. Narrower exceptions or no checked exceptions are fine. This ensures callers who handle the superclass exception contract still work with the subclass.

Example: superclass throws IOException, subclass may throw FileNotFoundException or nothing, but not Exception.
Common Mistake

Attempting to reduce visibility or widen checked exceptions will fail at compile time. Treat exception and visibility rules as part of the method contract.

screens.title: The @Override Annotation
screens.narratorSegment: The @Override annotation is a simple but powerful tool. When you put it above a method, you tell the compiler: I intend for this method to override a method in a superclass. The compiler then verifies that intent. If the method signature does not match any method in the superclass chain, the compiler reports an error. This prevents a very common bug: a typo in the method name or a changed parameter list that silently creates a new method (overloading) that never replaces the superclass behavior. Using @Override improves readability because other developers immediately see your intent, and it speeds up code reviews and refactors because the compiler enforces the relationship. A typical example: you think you override displayItemDetails but accidentally change the parameter or return type — without @Override you'd compile, run, and find the superclass method still executes. With @Override you'll get a compile-time error. Habitually annotating intended overrides is recommended practice; it increases confidence and prevents subtle runtime surprises. The @Override Annotation means annotating intended overrides yields compile-time checks that enforce your intent and catch typos or signature mistakes early.. In practical terms, why annotate and what compiler checks it performs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › @Override Annotation
What it does

@Override instructs the compiler to verify that the annotated method overrides a method from a superclass. If it does not, the compiler reports an error, preventing accidental overloading or new-method creation.

// Intended override
@Override
public void displayItemDetails() { /* ... */ }

// If signature mismatches, compiler will fail and alert you.
Why it's recommended
  • Surfaces typos and signature mismatches at compile time.
  • Makes developer intent explicit for maintainers.
  • Speeds safe refactoring when superclasses change.
Misconception: @Override is mandatory — it isn’t, but leaving it out removes a valuable safety check.

screens.title: Using super.method() to Extend Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Calling super. method() inside an overriding method is a common pattern when you want to reuse shared logic from the superclass and then append subclass-specific behavior. It helps avoid duplicating code and keeps common responsibilities centralized. Consider the LibraryItem example: the superclass displayItemDetails prints title, ID, and status. Book overrides displayItemDetails but begins by calling super. displayItemDetails(), which prints the shared fields, and then Book prints the author and page count. This pattern is safer than copying the superclass code into every subclass because changes to common display logic need only happen in the superclass. One misconception is thinking super always fully executes the old behavior — sometimes you want to call super after subclass logic or not call it at all if you intend a complete replacement. Choose the pattern that best preserves invariants: call super first to maintain a consistent header or call super last if the subclass needs to validate or prepare data beforehand. The habit to form is: prefer reuse via super when there is shared behavior, and document the intent with @Override so reviewers understand the design.

keyIdea.title: Extend vs Replace
keyIdea.text: Call super.method() when you want to reuse common logic and then add subclass details; omit it for full replacements.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › super.method()
Pattern: reuse then extend
// Superclass
public void displayItemDetails() {
  System.out.println("Title: " + title);
  System.out.println("Item ID: " + itemID);
  System.out.println("Status: " + (isBorrowed ? "Borrowed" : "Available"));
}

// Subclass
@Override
public void displayItemDetails() {
  super.displayItemDetails(); // reuse common fields
  System.out.println("Author: " + author);
}
When to call super
  • Call first when superclass provides header or required state setup.
  • Call last when subclass needs to prepare or validate data first.
  • Omit when the subclass fully replaces the behavior and shared logic is irrelevant.
Key Takeaway

Use super to avoid duplication and to keep common logic centralized; choose call order to preserve invariants.

screens.title: Overriding vs Overloading
screens.narratorSegment: Overriding and overloading are different tools with different purposes. Overriding replaces or extends a superclass method in a subclass while keeping the same signature so calls through superclass references are dispatched to the subclass at runtime. Overloading provides multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists, usually within the same class, and it is resolved at compile time. A typical pitfall is accidentally creating an overloaded method when you intended to override — for example, changing a parameter type or adding an extra parameter results in a new method that never replaces the superclass implementation. That bug is silent unless you use @Override or test via a superclass reference. Concrete example: if Shape has public String getName(), and Circle defines public String getName(String type), that is overloading, not overriding, and callers expecting getName() through a Shape reference will still see the superclass result. To avoid this, always verify signatures and annotate overrides. The final takeaway is: overriding affects runtime behavior and polymorphism; overloading provides convenience variations resolved at compile time. Overriding vs Overloading means overriding changes runtime dispatch for subclass instances; overloading offers different compile-time options with same name but different parameters.. In practical terms, a clear contrast with examples and a pitfall to avoid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Overriding changes runtime dispatch for subclass instances; overloading offers different compile-time options with same name but different parameters.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Overriding vs Overloading
Overriding (runtime)
Same signature in subclass; runtime dispatch chooses the subclass implementation for superclass-typed references.
// Overriding
class Shape { public String getName() { return "Generic Shape"; } }
class Circle extends Shape { @Override public String getName() { return "Circle"; } }
Shape s = new Circle();
System.out.println(s.getName()); // prints "Circle"
Overloading (compile-time)
Same name but different parameters; resolved at compile time and does not affect runtime dispatch of superclass calls.
// Overloading
class Shape {
  public String getName() { return "Generic Shape"; }
  public String getName(String type) { return type; } // overload
}
Pitfall

Changing parameters when you meant to override creates an overload and leaves the original method unchanged for polymorphic calls. Use @Override to prevent this mistake.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Catch Them
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes learners make when overriding methods. First, typos in the method name or changes to the parameter list produce an overloaded or new method rather than an override. The result is often a silent bug because the original superclass method still runs for superclass-typed references. Second, changing the return type to an incompatible type or making the overriding method less accessible will cause compile errors. Third, widening checked exceptions in the overriding method breaks the exception contract and is disallowed. How do you catch these problems early? Use @Override for all intended overrides so the compiler can verify your intent. Run small tests that call methods via superclass references to confirm runtime behavior. Use code reviews to check access levels and declared exceptions. Finally, prefer calling super when you want shared behavior; this reduces duplicated code that might diverge over time. If you adopt these habits—annotate, compile, test via a superclass reference—you’ll find most overriding bugs disappear during development rather than appearing at runtime. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how subclasses change inherited behavior through method overriding and why that matters for polymorphism and clean code. Overriding lets a subclass provide a specific implementation for a method defined in its superclass while keeping the same method signature, which preserves polymorphic calls. For example, an Animal class can define a generic makeSound method while Dog and Cat subclasses override it to bark or meow. You will also learn the practical rules that govern overriding: matching signature, compatible return types including covariant returns, access modifier constraints, and rules about checked exceptions. Equally important is the @Override annotation — it tells the compiler you intend to override and prevents subtle errors that would otherwise create overloaded or new methods by accident. Throughout the screens you’ll see concrete code examples, a hands-on vehicle exercise, and common mistakes you can spot during code reviews. By the end, you’ll be able to override methods correctly, call super when appropriate, and use @Override to catch errors early. Think about one superclass method you would want to change in your own codebase — how would a subclass improve it?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to tell overriding and overloading apart and apply the right technique in your code. You will practice writing subclass methods that match a superclass signature and use covariant return types when appropriate. You will also use the @Override annotation as a compile-time check so small typos or signature mismatches surface immediately instead of silently changing behavior. Finally, you will learn the rules about access modifiers and checked exceptions in overriding and how to call the superclass implementation with super. method() to extend, not replace, inherited behavior. Each objective pairs a definition with a short why-it-matters example so you can see immediate value: for instance, overriding makeSound() in an Animal hierarchy makes polymorphic code expressive and predictable. These skills reduce runtime surprises and make code easier to maintain and review. Practice and the included hands-on exercises will reinforce how to recognize mistakes and protect your intent with @Override.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills and mental checks you should adopt. You will practice calling super. method() from a subclass to reuse and then augment behavior. For example, a Book subclass can call super. displayItemDetails() to print common fields and then add author and page-count lines. You will also learn to identify common mistakes: mismatched parameter lists cause overloading, wrong return types break overriding unless covariant returns are used, and making the overriding method less accessible will generate compile errors. Finally, you'll run a brief vehicle exercise that starts with a Vehicle superclass and asks you to override a startEngine method in Car and Motorcycle, calling super first and then adding subclass messages. That exercise shows how overriding supports code reuse and clearer runtime output. Adopt two habits: annotate intended overrides with @Override, and run a compile to confirm your intent. These habits catch many class-hierarchy bugs early.

Method overriding is the mechanism where a subclass provides a specific implementation for a method already declared in its superclass, keeping the same method signature. The purpose is to let different concrete types respond differently to the same polymorphic call. For a concrete picture, imagine an Animal class with a makeSound method that prints a generic message. A Dog subclass overrides makeSound to print a bark string, and a Cat subclass overrides it to print a meow. When code holds a reference of type Animal to a Dog instance and calls makeSound, the Dog version runs because Java uses dynamic dispatch at runtime. Overriding supports polymorphism: you can write generic code that treats many subclasses uniformly while each subclass implements its own behavior. A common misconception is thinking that simply defining a method with the same name in a subclass is enough; the signature must match exactly to be overriding, or else you’ve silently created a different method. This silent creation of a new method is dangerous because calls through superclass references will not use your intended implementation. Takeaway: overriding preserves the method contract while changing behavior — that contract is what lets polymorphism work reliably.

For a method in a subclass to override a superclass method, the signature must match: same method name and the same number, types, and order of parameters. The return type must be compatible. Java allows covariant return types: the overriding method may return a subtype of the original return type. For example, if a superclass method returns java. lang. Number, a subclass override can return java. lang. Integer. This preserves substitutability because every Integer is a Number, but not every Number is an Integer. Another rule is that generic type erasure can affect signatures — but your practical check is simple: the compiler will accept a covariant return only when it is type-safe. A useful mental model is: overriding keeps the contract consumers expect, while a covariant return type narrows what the caller actually gets at runtime in a safe way. A common mistake is changing parameter types or order; that creates an overloaded method, not an overridden one, and calls through superclass references will still invoke the original method. Always compile and run a small test that calls the method via a superclass reference to confirm the override.

Two important constraints often catch learners by surprise: access modifiers and checked exceptions. When a subclass overrides a method, it cannot use a more restrictive access modifier than the superclass method. For instance, if the superclass method is protected, the subclass method can be protected or public, but not private. This rule maintains substitutability for callers with different visibility. For exceptions, an overriding method cannot declare checked exceptions that are broader than those declared by the overridden method. If the superclass method declares to throw IOException, the overriding method may declare to throw FileNotFoundException, which is narrower, or declare no checked exceptions. Declaring a broader checked exception would break callers that rely on the original contract. A helpful contrast: unchecked exceptions (runtime exceptions) are not checked by this rule, so they can be thrown freely, but you should still be careful to preserve A P I expectations. A common mistake is making an overriding method private or adding a broad checked exception; both generate compile-time errors. The safe habit is to mirror or relax visibility and restrict checked exceptions to compatible or narrower types.

The @Override annotation is a simple but powerful tool. When you put it above a method, you tell the compiler: I intend for this method to override a method in a superclass. The compiler then verifies that intent. If the method signature does not match any method in the superclass chain, the compiler reports an error. This prevents a very common bug: a typo in the method name or a changed parameter list that silently creates a new method (overloading) that never replaces the superclass behavior. Using @Override improves readability because other developers immediately see your intent, and it speeds up code reviews and refactors because the compiler enforces the relationship. A typical example: you think you override displayItemDetails but accidentally change the parameter or return type — without @Override you'd compile, run, and find the superclass method still executes. With @Override you'll get a compile-time error. Habitually annotating intended overrides is recommended practice; it increases confidence and prevents subtle runtime surprises. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Calling super. method() inside an overriding method is a common pattern when you want to reuse shared logic from the superclass and then append subclass-specific behavior. It helps avoid duplicating code and keeps common responsibilities centralized. Consider the LibraryItem example: the superclass displayItemDetails prints title, ID, and status. Book overrides displayItemDetails but begins by calling super. displayItemDetails(), which prints the shared fields, and then Book prints the author and page count. This pattern is safer than copying the superclass code into every subclass because changes to common display logic need only happen in the superclass. One misconception is thinking super always fully executes the old behavior — sometimes you want to call super after subclass logic or not call it at all if you intend a complete replacement. Choose the pattern that best preserves invariants: call super first to maintain a consistent header or call super last if the subclass needs to validate or prepare data beforehand. The habit to form is: prefer reuse via super when there is shared behavior, and document the intent with @Override so reviewers understand the design.

Overriding and overloading are different tools with different purposes. Overriding replaces or extends a superclass method in a subclass while keeping the same signature so calls through superclass references are dispatched to the subclass at runtime. Overloading provides multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists, usually within the same class, and it is resolved at compile time. To avoid this, always verify signatures and annotate overrides. The final takeaway is: overriding affects runtime behavior and polymorphism; overloading provides convenience variations resolved at compile time.
